openingProblem.problem: In 1928 the Soviet Union was still a peasant country. By 1941 it had built steel cities and an armaments industry that would help defeat Germany, but millions had died in famine and the countryside was exhausted. Was Stalin's economic revolution a success?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: success, failure, or both?
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: The First Five-Year Plan, 1928–1932
chunks.body:
In 1928 Stalin's leadership abandoned the gradualism of NEP for the **First Five-Year Plan** (1928–32), the most ambitious exercise in central planning ever attempted. Its aim was to make the Soviet Union an industrial power at astonishing speed. In February 1931 Stalin told managers that the USSR was a hundred years behind the advanced countries and had to make up the gap in ten years.

The planners of Gosplan worked backwards from targets set by the leadership. The "optimal" variant adopted in April 1929 demanded a 228 per cent rise in investment and a 335 per cent rise in electricity output. Coal output, 35 million tons in 1927–28, was to reach 75 million tons, and the target was later raised to 95–105 million. In December 1929 the leadership declared that the plan would be fulfilled "in its essentials" in four years.

Huge new projects symbolised the drive. **Magnitogorsk**, founded in 1929 around what became the world's largest steel plant, had 250,000 inhabitants by 1932, many living in tents and mud huts. Its builders included Komsomol enthusiasts, peasant recruits and deported "kulaks". To raise productivity, the regime promoted **shock workers** who exceeded their quotas; by 1930, 65 per cent of industrial workers were taking part, though "false shock work" was common.

The cost was immense. The rush, shortages and waste, the historian Lewis Siegelbaum writes, "proved lethal to millions of people". Yet the plan was declared a success, and it did make the Soviet Union one of the world's leading industrial countries.

This mattered because industrial growth was bought with impossible targets and human suffering, which meant that the Five-Year Plans were a success by the regime's measure and a disaster by many others.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: It made the USSR a leading industrial power.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Stalin justified speed by the need to catch up.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The pace caused waste and death.

chunks.title: Collectivisation and the war on the kulaks, 1929–1933
chunks.body:
Industrialisation needed grain to feed the growing towns. After grain procurements fell short in 1927–28, Stalin abandoned the market. **Collectivisation** rested on two beliefs: that large, mechanised collective farms would be more efficient and easier to extract grain from, and that the **kulaks** (better-off peasants) were a "class-alien" enemy who had to be eliminated. Collectivisation therefore went hand in hand with **dekulakisation**.

By June 1929 only one million of some 25 million peasant households had joined collective farms. Then the pace was forced. A decree of 5 January 1930 called for collectivising most farms in the main grain regions by the autumn. Brigades of urban workers went to the villages; those labelled kulaks faced confiscation, deportation, the labour camps or execution. By March 1930 about 55 per cent of households had nominally joined. Stalin then blamed local officials for being "**dizzy with success**", and within three months over half of them left. But fines and compulsory sales of property drove many back: by mid-1932 61.5 per cent of households were in collective farms. Machine-tractor stations gave the state technical, and from 1933 political, control of the countryside.

Peasants resisted by slaughtering their livestock, by riots led by women, by theft and by working slowly. Procurement quotas exceeded what most farms could produce. After a poor harvest in 1932, famine struck Ukraine, the Lower Volga and the North Caucasus. The authorities blamed kulak sabotage and gave food to the towns and the army first. At least five million people died.

This mattered because the state took control of the peasantry and its grain at the price of famine, which meant that collectivisation served industrialisation while devastating Soviet agriculture.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Ideology against kulaks also drove it.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The pace was forced by violence.

chunks.title: Workers, Stakhanovites and discipline, 1932–1941
chunks.body:
The regime relied on both rewards and punishment to make workers produce. Shock workers received better canteen meals, scarce goods, housing and holiday vouchers. On 31 August 1935 the miner **Aleksei Stakhanov** cut 102 tons of coal in a six-hour shift, fourteen times his quota. The party turned him into a model, and the **Stakhanovite movement** rewarded record-breakers with high piece-rate earnings and consumer goods. Yet Stakhanovites were often resented by fellow workers, especially when output norms were raised in early 1936, and engineers who warned that "recordmania" disrupted production were accused of sabotage.

Punishment grew harsher. From November 1932 a single day's unexcused absence could cost a worker his job, his ration card and his housing. Labour books followed in 1938, and a decree of **26 June 1940** in effect made quitting a job or absenteeism a crime. Rationing was in force from 1929 to 1935.

The countryside settled into the collective-farm system, entrenched by the Second Kolkhoz Charter of 1935, which let peasants keep small private plots. At the Seventeenth Party Congress of 1934, the "Congress of Victors", the leadership celebrated a good harvest and new factories. But the human cost was concealed: the census of 1937 showed the population had grown by only 7.2 million since 1926 instead of the expected 37.6 million, so it was suppressed and its director arrested.

This mattered because the regime combined material incentives with coercion, which meant that output rose while the true social cost of the plans was hidden.

chunks.title: Success or failure? Historians and the famine
chunks.body:
Was Stalin's economic revolution a success? By the regime's own measure, yes: the First Five-Year Plan made the Soviet Union one of the world's leading industrial countries. But agriculture was another story. Lewis Siegelbaum concludes that collectivisation was only "a partial victory for the state over the peasantry": it brought peasants under state control and made them dependent on the machine-tractor stations, but administrative incompetence, under-investment and peasant alienation produced extremely low productivity, so that agriculture became "a net drain on economic growth".

The **famine of 1932–33** is the most bitterly debated question. Historians agree that the state's policies were central. **Stephen Wheatcroft** points out that the harvests of 1931 and 1932 were bad, "largely but not wholly" for natural reasons, but gives more weight to the government's "ill-conceived policies"; he calls its conduct criminal acts of fraud and manslaughter, though not genocide. **J. Arch Getty** reports that most scholars working in the new archives see the famine as the result of "Stalinist bungling and rigidity rather than some genocidal plan". The economist **Michael Ellman** criticises this approach for defining intent too narrowly: a regime that knows its policies will cause mass death, he argues, can be held to have intended it.

This mattered because the judgement on Stalin's economy depends on the criterion used, which meant that the same policies can be seen as a modernising success or as a crime against the peasantry.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Industrialisation succeeded by the regime's measure.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Its targets were never met in full.
It gave the state political control.

segments.text: Stalin's policies weighed on both workers and peasants, but far more heavily on the peasants.
Workers faced dismissal and eviction for a day's absence from 1932, whereas peasants faced deportation as kulaks and, in 1932–33, a famine in which the authorities fed towns first.
This meant that workers, though coerced, could gain rewards as shock workers or Stakhanovites, while peasants had no comparable incentives.
However, the two groups overlapped: Magnitogorsk's workforce included peasant recruits and deported kulaks living in tents and mud huts.
Both groups therefore suffered, but the peasants paid the higher price for industrialisation.

essayQuestions.text: To what extent was coercion the main method used to increase industrial production in the Soviet Union between 1928 and 1941?

decodeKey.verb: To what extent: judge how far
decodeKey.judgement: Did coercion outweigh planning and incentives?

modelPlan.thesis: Coercion was the main method, from labour-discipline laws to forced labour, but the regime also relied on central planning with ambitious targets and on incentives through shock work and Stakhanovism.
modelPlan.counter: False shock work and 'recordmania' disrupted production.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Main method? Coercion made workers keep the pace that planning set; incentives were secondary.

segments.text: Soviet industry grew through a combination of planning, incentives and coercion.
Gosplan set targets backwards from the leadership's ambitions, Stakhanov's 102-ton record of 1935 launched a movement of rewarded record-breakers, and from 1932 absence could cost a worker his job.
This meant that every worker faced both reward and threat, so production rose despite poor conditions.
However, false shock work and 'recordmania' disrupted production, and Stakhanovites were resented by fellow workers.
Coercion and planning were therefore the main methods, with incentives that often undermined efficiency.

essayQuestions.text: Evaluate the significance of the Stakhanovite movement for Soviet industry between 1935 and 1941.

decodeKey.verb: Evaluate: weigh strengths and limits, then judge
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The significance of the Stakhanovite movement

modelPlan.thesis: The Stakhanovite movement was significant as propaganda and as an incentive, rewarding record-breakers with high earnings, but it disrupted production, provoked resentment and led to higher norms and scapegoating.
modelPlan.counter: The movement continued into the war and was later exported to eastern Europe.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Significant how? As a symbol of the new Soviet worker more than as a source of output.

segments.text: The Stakhanovite movement mattered more as propaganda than as a source of production.
Stakhanov's 102-ton record of 31 August 1935 was hailed as a world record, and Stakhanovites were rewarded with high piece-rate earnings and consumer goods.
This meant that the regime could present a model of the new Soviet worker, so the movement spread rapidly in autumn 1935.
However, fellow workers resented Stakhanovites, especially when norms were raised in 1936, and engineers who warned of disruption were scapegoated.
The movement was therefore significant as a symbol, but it often damaged the production it was meant to raise.
